title: Airline passengers (1949-1960)
teaches: The classic series. Strong trend AND multiplicative seasonality — the textbook case for a log transform before SARIMA or Holt-Winters. The values are whole numbers of passengers; the app treats them as continuous, which is what forecasting packages do, but you can switch to the count branch in Column mapping to discuss it.

title: US accidental deaths (1973-1978)
teaches: Additive seasonality with a mild downward trend, and no obvious heteroskedasticity — the counter-example to AirPassengers.

title: Canadian lynx trappings (1821-1934)
teaches: A ~10-year population cycle with no fixed calendar: it is a CYCLE, not seasonality. Great for practising spectral analysis and log transforms.

title: Internet usage per minute (100 observations)
teaches: A short, strongly trending series where automatic ARIMA order selection is unreliable — a lesson in small-sample caution.
expect: strong trend, no seasonality, n small

title: Johnson & Johnson quarterly earnings
teaches: Quarterly data with growing seasonal amplitude — the case where a log transform stabilises the seasonality itself.

title: Yearly sunspot numbers (1700-1988)
teaches: A long record where the 11-year cycle drifts in length and amplitude. Shows why 'seasonality' must be distinguished from 'cyclicity'. Monthly sunspot numbers are counts, but yearly aggregates with this much dispersion behave as a continuous variable.

title: Australian beer production (quarterly)
teaches: Clean quarterly seasonality on a stable level. A gentle first encounter with seasonal differencing.

title: Daily electricity demand (2 years, synthetic but realistic)
teaches: Two seasonalities at once (weekly + yearly) — the case that needs MSTL or TBATS, and where a single-period STL under-fits.

title: Monthly retail sales (7 years, synthetic)
teaches: A trend plus a two-harmonic seasonal pattern: useful for comparing SARIMA with Fourier-term ARIMAX.

title: Monthly reported cases (Poisson-generated counts)
teaches: COUNT data from a Poisson process with a mild trend and seasonality. Poisson or negative-binomial models apply; MAPE is meaningless here, and a variance-stabilising transform is needed before any ARIMA attempt.

title: Spare-parts demand (intermittent, 72% zeros)
teaches: INTERMITTENT demand. Croston/TSB beat ARIMA here, and MASE — not MAPE — is the honest metric. A tool that offers ARIMA on this is misleading you.

title: Series with a structural break (level shift in 2015)
teaches: A single level shift fakes a unit root for ADF. Zivot-Andrews and Quandt-Andrews should find it; plain differencing hides it.
expect: level shift, candidate spurious unit root

title: Pure random walk (200 steps)
teaches: There is nothing to model but the last value: the naive forecast IS the correct answer, and any 'significant trend' you find is spurious.

title: White noise (no pattern at all)
teaches: The null case. A good tool must be willing to say 'no model is needed' — if yours always finds structure here, it is overfitting.

title: Retail units with promotion days (36 months x 3 years)
teaches: A second column that genuinely drives the first: every promotion day is worth about 88 units. A model that ignores it cannot reach the accuracy of one that uses it, and the future promotion plan is known in advance, so the scenario is realistic.
expect: trend + season + a promotion effect that is visible in the residual autocorrelation

title: Aftershock sequence: 456 event timestamps, no value column
teaches: Event data is a different kind of object. Each row is one occurrence, so the only observable quantity is the gap to the next one — and these gaps are far shorter right after an event, which is exactly what a Hawkes branching ratio measures. The timestamps carry times of day, because a continuous-time model cannot separate events recorded only to the day.
expect: bursts of events with a decaying rate after each one; Hawkes should beat renewal on AICc

title: Machine service visits: 95 event timestamps, near-regular gaps
teaches: The control for the aftershock file. Events here are roughly evenly spaced with no clustering, so a renewal model is the right description and a self-exciting one should find almost no branching — the comparison is only meaningful if both can lose.
expect: gaps with low dispersion around 9 days; renewal preferred, branching ratio near zero

title: Weekly returns with volatility clustering (741 weeks)
teaches: The mean is close to zero and essentially unpredictable; the *spread* is not. Calm stretches follow calm stretches, then a bad week is followed by worse ones. This is the series the volatility family exists for. Fitted here, the mean path is flat — which is the honest answer — and the variance path is the deliverable: it starts well above the long-run level because the sample ends in a turbulent stretch, and decays back to it. A constant-variance model would report one interval width for every step, too narrow exactly when it matters.
expect: ARCH-LM rejects strongly on the mean-adjusted series; the t versions beat the Gaussian ones on AICc; persistence near 0.95 with a variance path converging down to the long-run level

title: Store traffic and marketing spend (15 years monthly)
teaches: Two series that wander together: both trend up over fifteen years, but the gap between them mean-reverts, so they are cointegrated rather than merely correlated. This is the dataset the multivariate branch exists for. Match it lightly against the independent-walk case: two unrelated trending series look just as impressive on a scatter plot and produce significant level Granger tests, which is why the VAR quotes a differenced second opinion and the VECM checks its own relation before believing it.
expect: two non-stationary series with a stationary linear combination (rank 1)
